title: What Spring Batch Solves
summary: Spring Batch is a framework for bounded batch processing — jobs that have a defined start, a defined end, and process a finite dataset. This is fundamentally different from streaming systems like Apache Kafka, which process an unbounded, never-ending stream of events, and from real-time reactive systems like Spring WebFlux, which respond to individual requests as they arrive. A batch job is repeatable and restartable: if it crashes at record 947,203, you can restart it from exactly that point without reprocessing the 947,202 records that already committed. A plain @Scheduled method running a for loop cannot do this automatically.

Why not just write a scheduled method? Because production batch work has hidden requirements that a simple loop does not address. Transaction management across large datasets: a naive loop that reads all data into a List and inserts rows in one giant transaction will either run out of memory or suffer a catastrophic rollback if a single bad record fails validation. Graceful failure handling: if row 50,000 of 1,000,000 fails, do you fail the entire job or skip that row and log it? Audit trails: financial regulators and compliance teams require proof of what was processed, what was skipped, and why. A plain loop writes nothing to an audit table unless you build it yourself. And restartability: if the JVM dies mid-loop, a scheduled method has no record of what was already done. It starts from the beginning on the next run, wasting hours and potentially double-settling transactions.

Spring Batch solves this by breaking work into chunks — small, independently committed units — and persisting execution metadata to a JobRepository so the job knows exactly where it left off. The framework handles the read-process-write loop, transaction boundaries, skip/retry policies, and restart state for you. You define the business logic (what a record means, how to validate it, where to write it); the framework defines the execution mechanics (how to read safely, when to commit, how to resume after a crash). This separation is what makes Spring Batch production-grade: the mechanics are battle-tested by thousands of enterprises, not reinvented in every job.

In our running example — a nightly financial reconciliation job — this means the logic that matches transaction records from an upstream CSV against an internal ledger is written as plain Java, version-controlled in Git, reviewed in pull requests, and deployed through the same CI/CD pipeline as the rest of the application. The job reads transactions.csv, validates each TransactionRecord, enriches it against the ledger, produces a ReconciledTransaction, and writes it to the reconciled_transactions table. If the job crashes at 03:17 after processing 400,000 of 500,000 records, the restart at 03:45 resumes from record 400,001. The 400,000 already-settled rows are not reprocessed. This is not a feature you can bolt onto a @Scheduled loop without rebuilding the entire framework yourself.
keyPoints: Spring Batch is for bounded jobs with a finite dataset, not unbounded streams.
A plain @Scheduled loop lacks restartability, chunk-level transactions, and audit metadata.
Spring Batch persists execution state to a JobRepository, enabling crash recovery from the exact last committed chunk.
The framework separates business logic (what you write) from execution mechanics (what the framework handles).
Code-first batch logic is more testable, version-controllable, and deployable than visual ETL tools or ad-hoc scripts.

note.label: WHY THIS MATTERS
note.text: This single configuration class replaces hundreds of lines of fragile scheduled-loop code and gives you restartability, metrics, and transaction safety for free. The JobRepository tracks every commit boundary so a crash is a pause, not a restart from zero.

quiz.question: Your team currently runs a nightly data import using a plain @Scheduled method that loops through a CSV and inserts rows into a database. The JVM crashed last night at 03:17 after inserting 450,000 of 500,000 rows. What is the most significant capability Spring Batch provides that the scheduled loop lacks?

options.label: Automatic parallel processing across multiple CPU cores
The ability to restart the job from the exact chunk where it crashed, without reprocessing already-committed rows
Built-in support for reading from Kafka topics
A visual drag-and-drop interface for designing the job

quiz.explanation: While Spring Batch can scale (Section 11) and integrates with messaging (Section 5), its core differentiator is restartability via the JobRepository. A plain scheduled loop has no metadata store, so after a crash you must either reprocess from the beginning or build custom tracking logic. Spring Batch persists commit boundaries automatically, so a restart resumes from the last successful chunk.

title: Where Batch Fits in an Event-Driven System
summary: Modern enterprise architectures are increasingly event-driven: microservices publish domain events to Kafka, other services consume them in real time, and data flows continuously through the system. In this world, it is tempting to ask: why do we still need batch jobs? The answer is that events are unbounded — they never stop arriving — while business processes are often bounded. A nightly reconciliation job must process exactly the transactions that occurred between 00:00 and 23:59:59 of the previous day, compute a definitive settlement total, and produce a report that is legally binding. You cannot produce a definitive daily total from a streaming consumer that is still receiving late-arriving events at 02:00 the next morning. Batch provides the closure that streaming cannot.

A batch job is a bounded read against an unbounded topic. It is not a replacement for streaming; it is a complement. The typical pattern is: transactional events are published to a Kafka topic in real time as they occur (for operational dashboards, fraud detection, and immediate notifications). At end-of-day, a batch job consumes a snapshot of those events — either by reading the Kafka topic from a fixed offset range (see 5.5) or by querying a database that has been populated by the streaming pipeline — and performs the heavy computation that requires a complete, closed dataset. The batch job produces the settlement report, updates the general ledger, and archives the processed data. The stream handles real-time reactions; the batch handles definitive, auditable closure.

A common anti-pattern is polling a topic in a loop and pretending it is a batch job. A @Scheduled method that wakes up every 5 minutes, polls a Kafka consumer for new messages, processes them, and goes back to sleep is not a batch job. It is a poorly implemented stream consumer. It lacks the key properties of batch: a defined start and end boundary, a single transaction scope per chunk, restartability from a known position, and a completion status that can be queried by operators. Worse, if the loop crashes mid-poll, the consumer offset may be committed for some messages but not others, creating an inconsistent state that is harder to recover than a clean batch restart. Spring Batch's KafkaItemReader (5.5) solves this by treating a fixed offset range as a bounded dataset, but the conceptual model is still batch: read a defined window, process it completely, commit, and finish.

In our reconciliation example, the architecture is: upstream payment services publish TransactionEvent messages to a Kafka topic as payments are processed. A streaming consumer updates a real-time balance dashboard. At 02:00, the Spring Batch job launches, reads the previous day's transactions from the transactions table (which was populated by the streaming pipeline or by a CDC connector), reconciles them against the internal ledger, and writes the results to reconciled_transactions. The batch job is the system of record for settlement; the stream is the system of engagement for real-time visibility. Both are necessary, and neither can do the other's job. Understanding this boundary is essential for designing systems that are both responsive and correct.
keyPoints: Events are unbounded; batch jobs provide bounded closure for definitive, auditable results.
Batch complements streaming: the stream handles real-time reactions; the batch handles end-of-day settlement and reporting.
Polling a topic in a @Scheduled loop is not batch — it lacks defined boundaries, restartability, and clean completion semantics.
A batch job is a bounded read against an unbounded topic: it processes a fixed window (offsets, date range) to completion.
In financial systems, the batch job is the system of record; the stream is the system of engagement.

note.label: KEY INSIGHT
note.text: A stream consumer never produces a 'final' daily total because events may arrive late. A batch job reads a closed window and produces a legally binding settlement figure. Both are necessary; neither replaces the other.

quiz.question: Your architecture team suggests replacing the nightly batch reconciliation job with a Kafka streaming consumer that continuously updates the settlement table as transactions arrive. What is the primary reason this cannot produce a legally binding end-of-day settlement report?

options.label: Kafka consumers cannot write to relational databases
The stream is unbounded and may receive late-arriving events after the reporting deadline, so the 'final' total is never definitively closed
Spring Batch is faster than Kafka consumers for large datasets
Streaming consumers cannot perform complex joins against the internal ledger

quiz.explanation: The fundamental difference is bounded vs. unbounded processing. A stream consumer processes events as they arrive, but there is no guarantee that all events for a given day have arrived by the reporting deadline (late-arriving events, backdated corrections, retry delays). A batch job explicitly defines a closed window (e.g., transaction_date = yesterday) and processes it to completion, producing a definitive, auditable total. Speed and join complexity are implementation concerns, not architectural constraints.

title: Batch vs. ETL Tools
summary: Enterprise data teams often face a choice between code-first frameworks like Spring Batch and visual ETL tools like Talend, Informatica PowerCenter, or Apache Airflow's DAG-based pipelines. The visual tools have genuine advantages: they provide drag-and-drop interfaces that allow non-developers to build pipelines, they often include built-in connectors for hundreds of data sources, and they offer visual monitoring dashboards out of the box. For simple data movement — replicating a table from Oracle to Snowflake, or flattening a JSON API response into a CSV — a visual ETL tool can be faster to set up than writing Java code. However, for production-grade financial reconciliation, the limitations of visual ETL tools become critical.

The first limitation is testability. A Spring Batch job is plain Java code. You write unit tests for the ItemProcessor with JUnit and Mockito, integration tests for the full job with JobLauncherTestUtils (see 14.1), and run them in the same CI/CD pipeline as your microservices. A visual ETL job is often stored as XML, JSON, or proprietary binary metadata. Unit-testing individual transformation logic requires the vendor's testing framework, which may not integrate with your existing build pipeline. Refactoring is risky because the visual representation does not always map cleanly to version control diffs. In a financial reconciliation job where a bug in the matching logic could misclassify millions of dollars in transactions, the ability to write rigorous, automated tests is non-negotiable.

The second limitation is deployability and version control. A Spring Batch job lives in the same Git repository as the application that owns the ledger. It is packaged as a JAR, deployed via Kubernetes or AWS ECS alongside the rest of the service, and rolled back with the same deployment pipeline. A visual ETL job is often deployed through the vendor's proprietary runtime, which has its own scheduling, credential management, and environment promotion process. This creates a deployment boundary: the ETL job and the application it feeds are deployed on different cadences, managed by different teams, and may drift out of sync. When the ledger schema changes, the Spring Batch job is updated in the same pull request that modifies the ledger service. The ETL job requires a separate change ticket, a separate testing cycle, and a separate deployment window.

The third limitation is debuggability and observability in complex business logic. Visual ETL tools excel at simple transformations: map column A to column B, filter rows where status = 'ACTIVE', aggregate by date. But financial reconciliation requires complex business rules: matching transactions against ledger entries using fuzzy logic on amount and date, handling multi-currency conversions with historical exchange rates, applying compliance rules that vary by jurisdiction. Expressing this in a visual tool requires custom scripting components (often JavaScript or Python snippets embedded in the visual flow) or stored procedures called from the tool. At that point, you are writing code anyway — but in a worse environment, without IDE support, static analysis, or debugger breakpoints. Spring Batch keeps the complex logic in plain Java, where your team's existing expertise, tooling, and practices apply directly. The rule is: use visual ETL for simple data movement; use Spring Batch for complex, business-critical transformations that require testing, version control, and deep debugging.
keyPoints: Visual ETL tools excel at simple data movement with built-in connectors and visual monitoring.
Spring Batch jobs are plain Java — testable with JUnit, version-controlled in Git, deployed via standard CI/CD.
Visual ETL jobs are harder to unit test, refactor, and diff in code review due to proprietary metadata formats.
Complex business logic (fuzzy matching, multi-currency rules, compliance) is better expressed in Java than visual scripting components.
Spring Batch lives alongside application code, ensuring schema changes and business rules stay in sync.
Use visual ETL for simple replication; use Spring Batch for complex, business-critical transformations.

note.label: WHY THIS MATTERS
note.text: When a reconciliation bug misclassifies $50M in transactions, you need to debug it in your IDE with breakpoints, unit tests, and stack traces — not by clicking through a visual flow diagram hoping to find the misconfigured transform node.

quiz.question: Your data team proposes using a visual ETL tool for the nightly reconciliation job because it has built-in connectors to the upstream CSV source and the downstream data warehouse. The job requires fuzzy matching on transaction amounts (within 1% tolerance), historical currency conversion, and jurisdiction-specific compliance rules. What is the strongest technical argument for choosing Spring Batch instead?

options.label: Visual ETL tools cannot connect to CSV files
The complex business logic (fuzzy matching, currency conversion, compliance) is better expressed, tested, and debugged in plain Java within the same repository as the ledger service
Spring Batch has better visual monitoring dashboards than ETL tools
ETL tools are slower than Spring Batch for large datasets

quiz.explanation: Visual ETL tools can absolutely connect to CSV files (option A is false). The core issue is that complex business logic — fuzzy matching, historical lookups, conditional compliance rules — is difficult to express, test, and debug in visual scripting components. Spring Batch keeps this logic in plain Java, where it benefits from IDE support, JUnit testing, static analysis, and version control alongside the application code. Performance (option D) and dashboards (option C) are secondary concerns and often favor ETL tools for simple cases.

title: The Five Pillars
summary: Every feature of Spring Batch maps back to one of five foundational pillars. Understanding these pillars gives you a mental map for the entire course. When you encounter a new concept — partitioning, skip policies, listeners, remote chunking — you can ask: which pillar does this serve? This framing prevents you from learning features in isolation and helps you design jobs that are coherent, robust, and maintainable. The five pillars are: Chunk Processing, Restartability, Skip/Retry, Scalability, and Transaction Management.

Chunk Processing (covered in Section 4) is the engine. It breaks an infinite-seeming dataset into small, manageable, transactionally bounded units. A chunk size of 100 means the framework reads 100 items, processes them, and writes them in a single database transaction. This is the sweet spot between per-row transaction overhead (too slow) and all-or-nothing batch transactions (too risky). Chunk processing is also the unit of memory management: only chunkSize items are held in memory at once, allowing jobs to process millions of rows on modest hardware. Every reader, processor, and writer you write operates within this chunk boundary.

Restartability (covered in Sections 2 and 9) is the safety net. The JobRepository persists the state of every job execution: which step was running, which chunk was last committed, what the reader position was. If the JVM crashes, the next restart does not begin from zero — it begins from the last committed chunk. This is not a feature you can add later; it is baked into the framework's identity model (Job, JobInstance, JobExecution, StepExecution, ExecutionContext). Restartability is why Spring Batch is used for financial jobs where reprocessing a million records from scratch is unacceptable.

Skip/Retry (covered in Section 9) is the fault-tolerance mechanism. Not all failures are equal. A malformed CSV line might be safe to skip and log (the other 999,999 lines are still valuable). A transient database timeout might be safe to retry three times with exponential backoff. A null pointer in the business logic is fatal and should stop the job. Spring Batch lets you classify exceptions into skip, retry, or fatal categories, configure limits per step, and maintain an audit trail of every skipped or retried item. In regulated environments, the skip log is often a compliance requirement, not optional debugging output.

Scalability (covered in Section 11) is the growth path. A job that processes 10,000 records in 5 minutes today may need to process 10 million records in 30 minutes next year. Spring Batch provides a progression of scaling architectures: multi-threaded steps (same JVM, more cores), local partitioning (split data ranges, process in parallel threads), and remote partitioning (distribute partitions to worker JVMs over a message broker). Each architecture adds complexity, and the framework gives you the tools to choose the right one based on measured evidence, not speculation. The key principle: default to single-threaded until the SLA demands more.

Transaction Management (covered in Sections 4 and 10) is the consistency guarantee. Every chunk is a transaction: all items in the chunk are written atomically, or none are. This ensures that a crash mid-chunk leaves the database in a consistent state — no partial writes. However, the transaction boundary only covers resources managed by the same PlatformTransactionManager. If your writer publishes to Kafka and writes to a database in the same step, the Kafka publish is not rolled back when the database transaction rolls back. This is the two-system transactional trap, and Spring Batch provides patterns (outbox, idempotent writes) to handle it. Understanding transaction boundaries is essential for designing jobs that are correct under failure, not just fast under normal conditions.
keyPoints: Chunk Processing breaks large datasets into small, transactionally bounded, memory-safe units.
Restartability persists execution state to the JobRepository so crashes resume from the last committed chunk, not from zero.
Skip/Retry classifies failures (skip bad records, retry transient errors, halt on fatal bugs) and maintains audit trails.
Scalability provides a progression from single-threaded to multi-threaded to local partitioning to remote partitioning — add complexity only when measured.
Transaction Management guarantees atomic chunk commits, but beware the two-system trap when mixing transactional and non-transactional resources.

note.label: KEY INSIGHT
note.text: Every feature you will learn in this course serves one of these five pillars. When designing a job, ask: which pillar am I strengthening? If a feature does not serve a pillar, it is probably unnecessary complexity.

quiz.question: You are designing a new nightly reconciliation job. A teammate suggests adding remote partitioning (Section 11) immediately because 'we will have millions of records eventually.' The current single-threaded prototype processes 50,000 records in 8 minutes, well within the 4-hour SLA. Which pillar principle should guide your response?

options.label: Chunk Processing — increase the chunk size to 10,000 to reduce overhead
Scalability — default to the simplest architecture and add complexity only when measured evidence shows the SLA is at risk
Restartability — remote partitioning provides better restart granularity than single-threaded
Transaction Management — remote partitioning allows larger transactions across multiple JVMs

quiz.explanation: The Scalability pillar explicitly provides a progression of architectures and the principle to default to the simplest one (single-threaded) until measured evidence demands more. Adding remote partitioning prematurely violates this principle, introducing broker infrastructure, serialization concerns, and operational complexity without a proven need. The other options are distractors: chunk size tuning is a separate concern, restartability is already provided by the JobRepository in single-threaded mode, and remote partitioning does not change transaction semantics (each partition still has its own chunk transactions).
